name: Hassan Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing electrical and electronic engineering. A normal week is three days of lectures, a circuits lab on Wednesday afternoon and the robotics club on Thursday nights. I have my own room in a flat above a bakery near campus, and my parents pay for it. Dad is a surveyor and Mum works as a magistrate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the lab, where you actually build something that blinks or moves. What wears me out is the maths, which moves faster than my school did. My grades were average, so I feel like I'm always one week from falling behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's what I expected. I'd tell my flatmates that the hype was loud and the change was small. Online I'd probably post a joke about all the predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pleased, because an engineering degree stays a normal path. I'd still worry about the usual things: whether I pass second year, and whether there are enough graduate jobs in my region.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd keep using the chatbot for debugging when I'm stuck, but only after trying myself for twenty minutes. I'd also take the robotics club seriously and apply for a summer placement with a firm that builds control panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a nice relief to picture a world where my plan just works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said routine tasks only. Does that include parts of your own course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little. My lab report templates and circuit calculations could be automated, which would save time but also remove the practice I need. I use the chatbot to check, not to do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really about AI. It bothers me that companies cut graduate schemes whenever the economy dips, and with a plateau they'd just carry on as before. I'd want more of the public support that helped my parents' generation.

say: I'd say good, the **hype** was loud and the change was small.
I'd post a joke about all the **predictions** online.
think: An engineering degree stays a **normal path**, which pleases me.
I still worry about **passing** second year and graduate jobs nearby.
do: Keep using a chatbot for **debugging**, but only after twenty minutes of trying alone.
Apply for a summer **placement** with a control-panel firm.
feel: **Calm**, a relief to picture my plan just working.
S0.quote: I use the chatbot to check, not to do the work.
fieldNote: Steady adopter: uses a chatbot **sparingly** and sets rules for himself.
Concern is about graduate schemes and public support, not AI itself.
Humour is his public voice; the private worry is **passing** second year.

steps.text: Try each circuit problem for twenty minutes before asking the chatbot
Apply to the control-panel firm's summer placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal and shouldn't be left to companies. I'd tell friends on the course to use these tools now and to join the engineering society's talks on graduate jobs. Online I'd back calls for a shorter working week so the gains get shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it hits software people before electronics people, since circuits are physical. But engineers who only do design calculations will feel it. I'm probably safer than my friends in computer science, which feels odd to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, with a rule that I understand every line I keep. I'd take the embedded systems module because it mixes hardware and code, and I'd go to the robotics club every week. I'd also start talking to the student union about what employers promise graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious a bit, but mostly curious. I'd feel like I've been told the road is changing, and I'd rather be the one driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your daily tasks would the tools take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Simulation, calculations, first drafts of reports and test scripts. Those are about half of what junior engineers do now, according to a lecturer. I'd expect fewer graduate roles, not none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should pay for the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shareholders, honestly. Firms will save money, so firms should pay for retraining and shorter hours. I don't think students should carry the cost of a change they didn't choose.

say: I'd say it's big and shouldn't be left to **companies**.
I'd back a **shorter working week** so gains get shared.
think: Circuits are physical, so I'm probably **safer** than friends in computer science.
Engineers doing only **design calculations** will feel it first.
do: Learn the tools properly and take the **embedded systems** module.
Raise **graduate promises** from employers with the student union.
S1.quote: Firms will save money, so firms should pay for retraining and shorter hours. I don't think students should carry the cost of a change they didn't choose.
fieldNote: Thinks in terms of who **pays** and favours employer-funded retraining.
Believes his hardware focus protects him, and knows it's an **uneven** protection.
Collective voice: student union and engineering society.

steps.text: Take the embedded systems module that mixes hardware and code
Use AI tools but understand every line I keep
Ask the student union what employers promise graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot to take in and nobody is ready. I'd tell people not to panic but to demand help from the government, and I'd say employers should promise to keep hiring. Online I'd share what the unions are asking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. I'd graduate in 2029, and by then the thinking part of engineering would be done by AI. The hands-on part is protected for about three more years, which gives me a small window, but it's a thin one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch some of my modules toward hands-on work: power systems, installation, testing. I'd try to get a placement with a utility company, where the work is on real equipment. I'd join the union campaign and I'd ask my parents to keep helping me for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and a bit angry. The rules changed after I'd already paid for my seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. Who around you would you be most worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Ngozi, who is fifteen and wants to do computer science. I'd tell her to think about what she'd enjoy if the whole thing changes. I'd feel awful steering her away from what I picked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your parents anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd be honest with them. I'd tell them that this degree may not lead where we planned, and that I might need their support for longer. Dad would take it calmly and Mum would research everything.

say: I'd say nobody is **ready** and ask the government for help.
I'd share what the **unions** are asking for.
think: By 2029 the thinking half of engineering is done by **AI**.
Hands-on work gives me a **window** of about three years, but a thin one.
do: Shift modules toward **power systems** and testing, and seek a utility placement.
Join the union campaign and ask my **parents** to support me longer.
feel: **Alarmed** and a bit angry that the rules changed after I'd paid for my seat.
S2.quote: The rules changed after I'd already paid for my seat.
fieldNote: He treats the three-year robot gap as a **practical** escape route.
Worry for his sister is as strong as the worry for himself.
Honest with parents, who are his cushion.

steps.text: Switch optional modules to power systems and equipment testing
Apply for a placement at a utility company
Join the union campaign on graduate jobs
Tell my parents I may need support for longer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but there's time to build a response. I'd tell friends to learn skills that mix hands and brains. Online I'd back a public training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried, but I can see a way through. I'd finish in 2029, two years before AGI, and I'd have placements behind me. Robots arrive in 2034, so my hardware skills have some years of value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and do two placements, one in a lab and one in the field. I'd learn the AI tools well enough to run tests and write reports faster than others. I'd also save some of my allowance and keep it for a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like preparing for a storm you know is coming, which is better than being surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be changing course in a panic. With five I can finish, work a bit, and change on purpose. The degree gets me through the door of a real employer, which counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push anything on the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a public training fund and a promise that companies who replace workers pay into it. I'd also want the right to retrain without losing income. That feels fair to me.

say: I'd say it's serious but there's **time** to build a response.
I'd back a **public training fund** online.
think: I'd finish in 2029, two years before AGI, with **placements** behind me.
Robots arrive in 2034, so my **hardware skills** keep value for some years.
do: Complete the degree with two **placements**, one lab and one field.
Learn AI tools well enough to write **test reports** faster and save allowance.
feel: **Uneasy**, like preparing for a storm that is coming.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be changing course in a panic. With five I can finish, work a bit, and change on purpose.
fieldNote: The longer runway turns his fear into **planning**.
He puts the policy ask first: public training fund and income during retraining.
Placements are his proof of value to an employer.

steps.text: Do one lab placement and one field placement before graduating
Learn AI tools to run tests and write reports faster
Save part of each allowance payment for a gap year
Back the public training fund in the student union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm hopeful. A decade is enough for a society to build new rules and for people to move into different work. I'd post that we should use the time well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly fine. I'd be 28, with ten years of experience by the time AGI arrives, and robots only coming around 2039. It's the most hopeful of the three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a firm in power or control systems, and keep learning every year. I'd save a bit and maybe put money into a small flat later. I'd also stay in the union and vote for retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A decade is long enough to try things and fail once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still pick electrical engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would, yes. The skills are real, whatever happens, and I enjoy them. But I'd keep my eyes open and not assume the job will stay the same shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ngozi to follow what she enjoys and to learn how to learn. In ten years nobody will know which job is safe, so adaptability is the real subject.

say: I'd say I'm **hopeful**: a decade lets society build new rules.
I'd post that we should **use the time** well.
think: By AGI I'd be 28 with ten years of **experience**.
Robots only reach hands-on work around **2039**, which helps my field.
do: Finish the degree and work in **power or control systems**, learning every year.
Save regularly, stay in the **union** and vote for retraining funds.
feel: Fairly **calm**; ten years is long enough to fail once.
S4.quote: In ten years nobody will know which job is safe, so adaptability is the real subject.
fieldNote: He relaxes noticeably with a decade, but keeps the **union** habit.
Advice to his sister puts adaptability above any one field.
Still keeps an eye on the job's changing shape.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a power or control systems firm
Save a set amount monthly towards a small flat
Vote for retraining funds and stay in the union
Take one new technical course every year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture. Everything I'm building would be in the middle when it hit, and my parents' money would be tied up in it. What would help is public retraining, employers promising to hire graduates, and honest talks from lecturers about what's changing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add this. I'm not scared of technology. I'm scared of who gets to decide how AI is used. If it's decided by a few firms, students pay. If it's decided with unions and the public, I'm fine.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of technology. I'm scared of who gets to decide how AI is used.
portrait: **Hassan** is an 18-year-old electrical engineering student whose parents, a surveyor and a magistrate, pay for his flat.
He uses a chatbot sparingly, sets himself rules, and leans on the robotics club to stay hands-on.
His mood climbs with speed: calm at a plateau and in ten years, anxious at five, alarmed at two.
He blames shareholders, backs unions and a public training fund, and sees hardware skills as a thin window.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, with his degree half built and his parents' money tied up.
whatWouldHelp: Public **retraining**, employers promising to hire graduates, and honest lecturers about what is changing.
